newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb trial defense lectures jurors.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb trial defense lectures jurors.

text.p: The chief defence lawyer in the Oklahoma City bombing trial Monday grilled potential jurors about their views on the death penalty and lectured them on their duty to ignore media reports about the case.

Stephen Jones, worried that an avalanche of pre-trial publicity will prejudice jurors against defendant Timothy McVeigh, told potential jurors of their responsibility to listen only to the evidence and ignore anything else they had heard.
"If you serve, can you base the verdict ... solely on what you see and hear in this room?" Jones asked one jury candidate, a supermarket maintenance manager. "Yes, sir" the man replied.
"That's the system your dad fought for in the Korean War when he was in the Navy?" Jones said. "Yes sir," he repeated.

McVeigh, a 28-year-old Gulf War veteran, was accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building April 19, 1995, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds. He has pleaded not guilty but could face the death penalty if convicted.
The maintenance manager, like several others interviewed Monday, was aware of media reports that McVeigh had allegedly confessed to his lawyers -- reports denied by Jones.

A registered nurse, who heard reports that white supremacists were involved in the bombing, told Jones she was confident she could set aside opinions based on media reports. "Newspaper reports can be wrong?" Jones asked. "I agree," the woman answered.

The second week of jury selection began as slowly as the first. A total of 37 jury candidates had been questioned by day's end. Jury candidates cannot be seen by the public in court and they are identified only by a number.

A young cosmetics saleswoman said initially that the death penalty was never justified. "I don't feel any human being has the right to judge somebody. That's left up to a higher being," she said. But, questioned by Jones, she said she would be willing to set aside her personal view and consider the death penalty if McVeigh would be convicted.
Jury candidates are disqualified in capital cases if they cannot vote for execution under any circumstances.

A retired loan officer who served as a Marine during World War II said he believed the death penalty should always be used in cases of premeditated murder, but later conceded there could be other mitigating circumstances.

Another potential juror, a schoolteacher from a remote mountain town, said she was concerned about living alone in a big city like Denver if chosen to serve on the jury. She suggested that the elaborate security precautions surrounding the trial also worried her.
"The security arrangements (put in place for the jurors) let me know that you or the courts or someone thinks safety is an issue," she said.
Jones questioned all of the potential jurors Monday instead of sharing the task with others on the defence team as he did last week.

The judge and opposing attorneys were trying to whittle down a jury pool of around 350 people to 64. Each side could then challenge up to 23 jurors without giving a reason before settling on 12 jurors and six alternates. The process was expected to take up to four weeks.
McVeigh sat next to his lawyers in the courtroom paying close attention to the questioning. He is accused of planning the bombing with former Army buddy Terry Nichols, who will be tried separately.
